corpus_name: JUSTICE Section 27 Contract Act Precedent Corpus
data_policy: Every entry was verified against a free, public primary source (Indian Kanoon full-text judgments, Supreme Court of India judis portal). ratioSummary fields are editorial paraphrases for retrieval; the full judgment text lives at source.url. Never scraped from any paywalled database.

precedents.title: Percept D'Mark (India) (P) Ltd. v. Zaheer Khan
precedents.ratioSummary: A restrictive covenant operating after termination of the contract (here a right of first refusal after the agreement expired) is void under Section 27 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. Negative covenants can be enforced only during the subsistence of the contract; the English common-law test of reasonableness does not apply to post-termination restraints in India.

precedents.title: Superintendence Company of India (P) Ltd. v. Krishan Murgai
precedents.ratioSummary: A negative covenant restricting an employee from serving elsewhere during the period of employment is not in restraint of trade. A restraint operating after the termination of employment, however, is void under Section 27; Indian courts do not apply the English doctrine that partial or reasonable post-service restraints may be valid.

precedents.title: Niranjan Shankar Golikari v. The Century Spinning & Mfg. Co. Ltd.
precedents.ratioSummary: A negative covenant operating only during the subsistence of a contract of employment (exclusive service and protection of confidential spinning techniques) is not hit by Section 27, and an injunction may enforce it for the contract term. The case does not validate restraints that begin after the employment ends.

source.name: Indian Kanoon (free) + Supreme Court judis portal

precedents.title: Gujarat Bottling Co. Ltd. v. The Coca Cola Co.
statutes: Order XXXIX Rules 1 & 2, Code of Civil Procedure 1908
precedents.ratioSummary: A negative stipulation in a franchise agreement that operates during the period of the agreement (preventing the bottler from dealing with competing beverages) is not a restraint of trade under Section 27. The settled distinction holds: restraints during the contract term may be valid, restraints operating after termination are void.

precedents.title: Wipro Limited v. Beckman Coulter International S.A.
precedents.ratioSummary: Post-termination non-compete obligations between commercial parties are hit by Section 27 and leave no room for a judicial balancing or reasonableness test, following Percept D'Mark. Narrow non-solicitation obligations that protect an existing business relationship may be treated differently from a general bar on carrying on business.

precedents.title: Ambiance India Pvt. Ltd. v. Naveen Jain
precedents.ratioSummary: A clause restraining a former employee from soliciting the employer's customers for a limited period can be enforced where it protects confidential business connections, but a blanket bar on joining a competitor or carrying on any competing trade is void under Section 27. Knowledge acquired in employment cannot be equated with the employer's proprietary trade secrets without proof.

precedents.title: Desiccant Rotors International Pvt. Ltd. v. Bappaditya Sarkar & Anr
precedents.ratioSummary: An employer cannot obtain an injunction enforcing a post-service non-compete against a former manager; such restraints are void under Section 27 even where the employee joins a direct competitor. Protection is limited to genuine confidential information, not to restraining lawful competition itself.

precedents.title: Stellar Information Technology Pvt. Ltd. v. Rakesh Kumar & Ors
precedents.ratioSummary: An employer cannot dress up a non-compete as a confidentiality clause to restrain a former employee's trade; post-employment restraints remain void under Section 27. Obligations survive only insofar as they protect specific confidential information rather than bar competition itself.

precedents.title: K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (right to privacy)
altTitles: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India
precedents.ratioSummary: The right to privacy is a fundamental right intrinsic to Article 21 and Part III of the Constitution. The nine-judge bench expressly overruled M.P. Sharma (1954) and ADM Jabalpur (1976) to the extent they denied that status, and framed a proportionality test for state interference.

precedents.title: ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla
precedents.ratioSummary: Held (4:1) that during a National Emergency a person's right to move any court for enforcement of Article 21 remains suspended. Overruled by the nine-judge bench in Puttaswamy (2017); Justice H.R. Khanna's dissent is now the accepted position.

precedents.title: Central Board of Dawoodi Bohra Community v. State of Maharashtra
precedents.ratioSummary: The law laid down by a larger Bench of the Supreme Court is binding on any subsequent Bench of lesser or co-equal strength. A co-equal Bench doubting the correctness of an earlier Bench cannot overrule it, but must refer the matter to the Chief Justice for constitution of a larger Bench.

precedents.title: Kailash Nath Associates v. Delhi Development Authority
precedents.ratioSummary: Section 74 of the Contract Act awards only reasonable compensation not exceeding the penalty or sum named. Where damage or loss is capable of proof, it must be proved; forfeiture of earnest money or stipulated damages cannot occur in the absence of legal injury or proven loss.

precedents.title: D. Velusamy v. D. Patchaiammal
statutes: Section 2(f), Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005
precedents.ratioSummary: The Supreme Court recognized live-in relationships under Section 2(f) of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 as 'relationships in the nature of marriage', provided the couple held themselves out to society as akin to spouses, were of legal age to marry, and cohabited voluntarily for a significant period.
keywords: relationship in the nature of marriage

precedents.title: S. Khushboo v. Kanniammal & Anr.
precedents.ratioSummary: The Supreme Court held that two adult persons living together in a live-in relationship is not illegal and does not constitute any criminal offense. Consensual live-in relationships are constitutionally permissible and protected under Article 21 right to life and personal liberty.

precedents.title: V. Dhanapal Chettiar v. Yesodai Ammal
precedents.ratioSummary: A 7-judge Constitution Bench held that in premises governed by State Rent Control legislation, service of a contractual notice to quit under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act is not a condition precedent to an eviction petition. A landlord cannot forcefully or summarily evict a tenant and must establish one of the statutory grounds for eviction provided under the applicable State Rent Control Act before the competent authority.

precedents.title: Atma Ram Properties (P) Ltd. v. Federal Motors (P) Ltd.
statutes: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 - Order XLI Rule 5
precedents.ratioSummary: In premises governed by the Delhi Rent Control Act, eviction proceedings arose from alleged unlawful subletting. The Supreme Court held that once an eviction decree is passed, lawful tenancy terminates. Under Order XLI Rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an appellate court granting a stay of eviction has equitable jurisdiction to condition that stay on the tenant paying reasonable compensation or mesne profits for continued use and occupation during the pendency of the appeal.

precedents.title: Babu Manmohan Das Shah v. Bishun Das
statutes: U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947 - Section 3(1)(c)
precedents.ratioSummary: Under Section 3(1)(c) of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, a tenant is liable to eviction if they make alterations that materially alter the accommodation or are likely substantially to diminish its value. The question whether alterations are material is one of fact to be determined by the nature and extent of the structural changes made to the premises.
